subject: Business
title: Minimum Viable Product: Build, Measure, Learn
description: A fast breakdown of Minimum Viable Product: Build, Measure, Learn for builders.

hook.text: Dropbox's MVP was a 3-minute video. No product, no code — just a demo. Signups jumped from 5,000 to 75,000 overnight.

buildup.text: An MVP is the smallest version of a product that can test a key assumption with real customers.

discovery.text: Eric Ries's Lean Startup: build a small thing, measure customer response, learn, and iterate. Speed beats perfection.

twist.text: Most teams over-build MVPs. If you're not embarrassed by v1, you launched too late.

climax.text: Zappos' MVP: the founder photographed shoes in stores and listed them online.

punchline.text: Don't build the full vision. Build just enough to learn if the vision is right.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of a Minimum Viable Product?
options: To test a key assumption with real customers as quickly as possible
To launch a fully polished product

details.summary: A minimum viable product is the simplest version of a product that tests a core hypothesis with real users. The build-measure-learn loop uses MVP feedback to validate or invalidate assumptions quickly, avoiding wasting resources building full products nobody wants.
details.whyItMatters: Most startups fail because they build products nobody wants. The MVP approach tests market demand with minimal investment, ensuring that resources go toward validated ideas rather than untested assumptions about what customers need.
takeaways: An MVP tests core hypotheses with the simplest possible product version
Build-measure-learn cycles rapidly validate or invalidate business assumptions
Starting simple prevents wasting resources on features nobody wants

faq.question: What is the biggest mistake companies make with MVPs?
faq.answer: Building too much. Teams add features thinking they need a polished product for users to evaluate. The most effective MVPs are embarrassingly simple. Dropbox validated demand with just a video demo. Zappos tested shoe e-commerce by photographing store shoes and buying them when ordered.

faq.question: When is an MVP approach not appropriate?
faq.answer: When safety is critical like medical devices or aviation. When brand reputation is paramount and a poor first impression is unacceptable. When the minimum product requires significant infrastructure investment before any version is viable, like telecommunications networks.
